paragraphs.text: Glucose/galactose malabsorption is an autosomal recessive disorder that begins in the first weeks of life. The intestine selectively fails to absorb dietary glucose and galactose, which causes severe diarrhea and dehydration. The disorder is usually fatal unless these sugars are removed from the diet (Turk et al., 1991; Martin et al., 1996). Intestinal biopsies have shown a specific defect in Na(+)-dependent absorption of glucose in the brush border (Turk et al., 1991).

paragraphs.text: Abdullah et al. (1996) reported 8 Arab children with glucose-galactose malabsorption from 8 different families. Six were Saudi Arabs and 2 were of other Arab nationalities. Their mean age at presentation was 10.6 months. All had had chronic watery diarrhea since birth and failure to thrive. The diagnosis was confirmed by laboratory studies, including small-bowel biopsy, histology, and small-bowel enzyme assay. One child had a renal stone at the first visit, and a second child was found to have one on follow-up.

paragraphs.text: Xin and Wang (2011) reported 33 patients with GGM from a large Old Order Amish pedigree. All affected individuals had classic watery diarrhea and dehydration. Other features at presentation were increased bowel sounds, a distended abdomen, vigorous nursing despite their illness, irritability, and apathy. When patients were correctly diagnosed and adequately managed, the diarrhea stopped immediately and they were quickly rehydrated, and they then grew and developed normally. When the disease was not recognized, the clinical course was prolonged.

paragraphs.text: Elsas et al. (1970) studied glucose transport in jejunal mucosa in vitro and in the kidney in vivo in a 3-year-old girl with congenital glucose-galactose malabsorption, her family, and 16 normal volunteers. Biopsy specimens from 6 normal controls and from the girl's asymptomatic 5-year-old brother accumulated glucose to 16 times the concentration in the incubation medium. The proband's mucosa could not concentrate glucose at any point during a 60-minute incubation. Both parents and a half sister had impaired glucose transport, with values between normal and those of the proband. In these 3 heterozygotes, glucose influx was impaired but glucose efflux from the mucosa was the same as in 3 normal controls. Kinetic analysis showed reduced capacity (Vmax) but normal affinity (Km) for intestinal glucose transport. All subjects accumulated fructose to a similar degree. Renal glucose titration showed a partial defect in renal glucose reabsorption in the proband. Her brother's titration curve was similar to those of 7 normal volunteers. Elsas et al. (1970) concluded that heterozygotes can be detected and have reduced glucose transport capacity, and that absent intestinal glucose transport is accompanied by partial impairment of renal glucose transport.
